title: Anemia: Find the Mechanism Before Treating the Number
bottomLine: Anemia is a sign, not a diagnosis. Confirm chronicity and severity, use MCV plus reticulocyte response and iron or hemolysis studies to identify the mechanism, and look for the source of iron loss rather than simply prescribing iron forever.
recognize: Iron deficiency often causes microcytosis but can be normocytic early.
A high reticulocyte response suggests blood loss or hemolysis; an inappropriately low response suggests impaired production.
Older adults and postmenopausal patients with iron deficiency require evaluation for occult blood loss or malignancy risk.
differentiate: Ferritin can be falsely normal or high with inflammation; interpret ferritin with the clinical context and transferrin saturation when needed.
Macrocytosis may reflect B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, medication effects or marrow disease.
assessment: Ask bleeding, menstrual and GI history, diet, pregnancy, medications, alcohol, chronic disease, neurologic symptoms and family or ethnic hemoglobinopathy history.
Assess hemodynamic stability, cardiopulmonary symptoms and evidence of active bleeding.
workup: CBC indices, reticulocytes, ferritin or iron studies and smear as guided by the pattern; add B12, folate, renal, thyroid or hemolysis studies when indicated.
Do not order broad marrow or genetic panels before basic mechanism-based evaluation.
management: Treat the cause and replace the deficient nutrient when present; oral iron is appropriate for many stable patients while IV iron is useful when oral therapy fails, is not tolerated or rapid repletion is needed.
Transfusion decisions should be based on clinical status, active bleeding, comorbidity and hemoglobin—not an arbitrary number alone.
medicationSafety: Iron can interact with levothyroxine and other medications; counsel on spacing and expected GI effects.
Transfusion has meaningful risks and is not first-line treatment for stable iron deficiency when iron therapy is effective.
redFlags: Chest pain or severe dyspnea from anemia
Hemolysis with renal or neurologic compromise
counselling: Explain that correcting hemoglobin does not finish the work if the source of blood loss remains unknown.
followUp: Recheck hemoglobin and iron response at an appropriate interval and investigate nonresponse for adherence, ongoing blood loss, malabsorption or wrong diagnosis.
examTrap: Prescribing iron for microcytosis without confirming iron deficiency or investigating why the patient is iron deficient.
oneLinePearl: Treat anemia by mechanism, not colour or hemoglobin alone.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Transfusion Medicine Recommendations 2026

title: Thrombocytopenia: Bleeding Risk and Dangerous Mimics
bottomLine: First confirm thrombocytopenia is real, then separate isolated immune or drug-related thrombocytopenia from systemic emergencies such as TTP, DIC, sepsis, HELLP or marrow disease. Bleeding and organ dysfunction matter more than the platelet count in isolation.
recognize: Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping can produce a falsely low automated count.
ITP often causes isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise preserved blood counts and no systemic coagulation disorder.
Thrombocytopenia plus hemolytic anemia, neurologic or renal findings is an emergency pattern for thrombotic microangiopathy.
differentiate: DIC usually occurs in a systemic illness with coagulation abnormalities and consumption; ITP is typically isolated.
Pregnancy-related thrombocytopenia ranges from benign gestational change to preeclampsia or HELLP.
assessment: Assess active bleeding, petechiae or mucosal bleeding, fever, neurologic and renal symptoms, pregnancy, heparin and other drug exposures, alcohol, liver disease and infection.
workup: Repeat CBC and smear; use coagulation, hemolysis, renal or liver testing according to the pattern.
Do not diagnose ITP without considering pseudothrombocytopenia and secondary causes.
management: Emergency bleeding or TTP, DIC, HIT or HELLP suspicion requires urgent acute-care and specialty management.

For adult ITP, treatment is individualized by bleeding and platelet count; Choosing Wisely Canada advises against IVIG as routine first-line therapy for asymptomatic ITP when corticosteroids are appropriate.
medicationSafety: Review antiplatelets, anticoagulants and drugs associated with immune thrombocytopenia.
Platelet transfusion is reserved for defined bleeding or procedure indications rather than every low count.
redFlags: Pregnancy with hypertension or liver abnormalities
counselling: Teach bleeding precautions and which OTC medications can increase bleeding risk while the cause is being clarified.
followUp: Trend the count and cause-specific markers; isolated mild stable thrombocytopenia and rapidly falling counts require different follow-up intensity.
examTrap: Treating presumed ITP before reviewing the smear for schistocytes or confirming the low count is not platelet clumping.
oneLinePearl: Low platelets plus sick organs is not routine ITP.

title: Inflammatory Arthritis: Refer Early, Test Selectively
bottomLine: Persistent objective synovitis is a referral diagnosis. Pattern, duration and examination drive the differential; RF, anti-CCP and ANA support specific clinical hypotheses but should not be ordered as a broad rheumatology screen.
recognize: Inflammatory arthritis typically causes prolonged morning stiffness, joint swelling, warmth and improvement with activity rather than only pain after use.
RA often produces symmetric small-joint synovitis; psoriatic and spondyloarthritis patterns may include enthesitis, dactylitis, axial symptoms, psoriasis, uveitis or IBD.
differentiate: Osteoarthritis produces activity-related pain and bony enlargement without persistent inflammatory synovitis.
Choosing Wisely Canada advises against ANA screening in patients without signs or symptoms suggesting an ANA-associated rheumatic disease.
assessment: Document exact swollen and tender joints, morning stiffness, psoriasis or nail disease, inflammatory back pain, uveitis, bowel symptoms, family history and systemic features.
Check function and pregnancy plans because disease-modifying therapy decisions depend on them.
workup: CBC, inflammatory markers and disease-specific serology can support the clinical picture; image selectively.
Do not delay rheumatology referral while waiting for serology when persistent inflammatory arthritis is clinically evident.
management: Early DMARD treatment improves outcomes in RA; the Canadian Rheumatology Association living RA guideline was updated in April 2026.
Use NSAIDs or short bridging anti-inflammatory therapy only as symptom control where safe; they do not replace disease-modifying treatment.
medicationSafety: DMARDs require infection, pregnancy and laboratory monitoring specific to the agent.
Long-term glucocorticoids carry major metabolic, bone and infection harms and should not become the default chronic plan.
redFlags: Vision symptoms or severe headache suggesting vasculitis
counselling: Explain why early specialist disease modification matters even if symptoms temporarily respond to NSAIDs or steroids.
followUp: Track objective inflammation and function, not pain alone, and ensure vaccination and infection-risk planning before immunosuppression.
examTrap: Ordering ANA, RF, anti-CCP and multiple autoimmune panels for nonspecific fatigue and body aches without objective inflammatory findings.
oneLinePearl: Synovitis earns rheumatology; serology does not create synovitis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Rheumatology Association RA Living Guideline update April 2026

title: Giant Cell Arteritis and Polymyalgia Rheumatica
bottomLine: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms in an older adult with inflammatory features raises giant cell arteritis. Threatened vision is a treatment-now problem; do not wait for biopsy or imaging before glucocorticoids when suspicion is high.
recognize: GCA can cause new temporal or diffuse headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, constitutional symptoms, polymyalgia symptoms and transient or permanent visual loss.
PMR causes bilateral shoulder or hip girdle aching and morning stiffness in older adults, usually with elevated inflammatory markers.
differentiate: PMR should not cause true focal weakness; weakness, CK elevation or neurologic findings suggest another diagnosis.
A normal ESR does not absolutely exclude GCA; interpret inflammatory markers with clinical probability.
assessment: Ask visual loss or diplopia, jaw claudication, constitutional symptoms, limb claudication and PMR symptoms; examine temporal arteries, pulses, vision and neurologic status.
workup: Obtain ESR and CRP plus CBC and baseline metabolic testing, but do not delay treatment for results when vision is threatened.
Arrange urgent confirmatory vascular imaging or temporal artery biopsy through local pathways.
management: Start high-dose glucocorticoid treatment urgently when GCA is strongly suspected, with emergency ophthalmology or hospital assessment for visual symptoms.
Treat PMR with lower-dose glucocorticoid therapy after excluding mimics and monitor response.
medicationSafety: Glucocorticoid treatment requires bone, glucose, infection and GI-risk planning and a taper strategy.
Steroid response alone is not definitive proof of PMR because many conditions transiently improve with glucocorticoids.
counselling: Explain that treatment may need to begin before confirmation because irreversible visual loss can occur.
followUp: Monitor symptoms, inflammatory markers and glucocorticoid toxicity and watch for large-vessel complications.
examTrap: Waiting for temporal artery biopsy before starting treatment in a patient with classic GCA symptoms and visual disturbance.
oneLinePearl: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms: protect vision before proving the pathology.

title: Cellulitis, Abscess, and Pseudocellulitis
bottomLine: Cellulitis is usually unilateral and clinical; bilateral red swollen legs should trigger pseudocellulitis thinking. A fluctuant abscess needs drainage, and uncomplicated drained abscesses do not always need antibiotics unless systemic illness, immune compromise or extensive surrounding cellulitis is present.
recognize: Cellulitis causes expanding erythema, warmth, tenderness and edema, usually without a discrete drainable collection.
Abscess produces focal fluctuance or purulent collection.
Stasis dermatitis, lymphedema, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis and gout commonly mimic cellulitis, especially when both legs are involved.
differentiate: Necrotizing infection causes disproportionate pain, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, bullae, anesthesia or crepitus and is an emergency.
DVT and acute gout may mimic cellulitis but require different testing and treatment.
assessment: Assess systemic illness, immune status, diabetes, edema or venous disease, portals of entry, purulence, rapid progression and pain severity.
workup: Uncomplicated cellulitis usually needs no imaging or blood culture; ultrasound can identify occult abscess when the exam is uncertain.
Culture purulent material when results can alter treatment or disease is severe or recurrent.
management: Use local antimicrobial guidance matched to nonpurulent versus purulent infection and severity.
Drain an abscess when indicated; antibiotics are added for systemic illness, significant cellulitis, immune compromise or other risk factors.
Do not routinely prescribe antibiotics for bilateral lower-leg redness and swelling without evidence of infection.
medicationSafety: Dose-adjust antimicrobials for renal function and check allergy history; avoid unnecessarily broad MRSA coverage when the syndrome does not support it.
counselling: Marking the erythema border and giving explicit progression return precautions can support safe outpatient care.
followUp: Reassess nonresponse because the diagnosis may be wrong, source control may be incomplete or resistant infection may be present.
examTrap: Diagnosing bilateral chronic red edematous shins as cellulitis and prescribing repeated antibiotics.
oneLinePearl: Bilateral red legs are usually not bilateral cellulitis.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Emergency Medicine Recommendations

title: Dangerous Rash: Skin Findings That Change Disposition
bottomLine: The first rash decision is not the exact dermatologic label; it is whether the patient has mucosal involvement, skin pain, systemic toxicity, purpura, blistering or rapid progression that signals a life-threatening infection, drug reaction or inflammatory emergency.
recognize: Skin pain, dusky targets, blistering and mucosal erosions suggest Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Nonblanching petechiae or purpura with fever or toxicity can signal invasive bacterial infection or vasculitis.
Generalized erythroderma, facial edema, fever and organ injury after a new drug can indicate severe drug hypersensitivity.
differentiate: Simple urticaria is transient and blanching; urticaria plus airway, respiratory, circulatory or severe GI symptoms is anaphylaxis.
Purpura does not blanch and needs hematologic, infectious or vasculitic assessment rather than an antihistamine trial.
assessment: Assess ABCs, fever and hemodynamics, skin pain, mucosa, blistering, medication timeline, immunization or infection context and systemic organ symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, renal or liver tests, cultures and skin biopsy or specialty assessment according to the suspected emergency; do not delay transfer for exhaustive outpatient testing.
management: Stop the likely culprit drug in severe cutaneous adverse reaction and arrange emergency dermatology, burn or hospital-level supportive care as appropriate.
Treat anaphylaxis with epinephrine first and invasive bacterial sepsis immediately.
medicationSafety: Never re-expose a patient to a drug implicated in SJS or TEN without expert justification.
Do not treat a severe drug eruption with outpatient antihistamines alone when mucosa or organs are involved.
counselling: After severe drug reaction, document the culprit and reaction clearly and provide the patient with medication-avoidance information.
followUp: Severe drug reactions require organ and sequelae follow-up after hospitalization.
examTrap: Calling a painful blistering rash with oral ulcers an allergy and sending the patient home with diphenhydramine.
oneLinePearl: Painful skin plus mucosa or toxicity is an emergency until proven otherwise.

title: Pigmented Lesions and Melanoma
bottomLine: A changing or suspicious pigmented lesion needs timely dermoscopic or biopsy-capable evaluation; do not reassure based only on colour or size. The ugly-duckling concept and evolution are often more useful than a rigid checklist alone.
recognize: ABCDE features include asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter and evolution, but melanomas can be small or amelanotic.
Nodular melanoma may grow rapidly and vertically and can appear as an evolving raised lesion rather than a classic flat ABCDE mole.
differentiate: Seborrheic keratoses and benign nevi can look irregular, but new change, bleeding or atypical features require examination rather than assumption.
Acral and subungual melanoma may occur on palms, soles or nails and should not be dismissed because of skin tone or sun exposure pattern.
assessment: Ask evolution, bleeding, itch or pain, personal and family skin-cancer history, immunosuppression and sun or tanning exposure.
Examine the lesion in context with the rest of the patient's nevi and regional nodes when concerning.
workup: Suspicious melanoma is diagnosed by appropriate full-thickness biopsy technique when feasible; avoid destructive treatment before diagnosis.
Routine population imaging is not a substitute for clinical skin examination.
management: Arrange prompt dermatology or surgical evaluation for suspicious lesions; definitive treatment and staging follow histopathology.
Counsel sun protection without implying melanoma only occurs in heavily sun-exposed fair skin.
medicationSafety: Not primarily medication-driven; review immunosuppression as a skin-cancer risk factor.
redFlags: New nodular pigmented or amelanotic growth
counselling: Teach self-monitoring for evolution and the ugly-duckling lesion and advise against indoor tanning.
followUp: Ensure pathology results are tracked and acted upon; a biopsy without closed-loop result review is incomplete care.
examTrap: Reassuring a rapidly changing 5-mm lesion because it is smaller than the classic 6-mm ABCDE teaching point.
oneLinePearl: Evolution beats diameter: a changing lesion deserves attention.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association patient and professional education

title: Sinusitis and Otitis: Antibiotics Only When the Pattern Fits
bottomLine: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral and uncomplicated otitis can often be observed in selected children. Use duration, severity, worsening pattern and examination findings rather than prescribing antibiotics for every cold, sinus pressure or red tympanic membrane.
recognize: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is more likely with persistent symptoms without improvement, severe onset or double-worsening rather than the first days of a typical viral URI.
AOM diagnosis requires middle-ear effusion plus inflammatory findings, not erythema alone.
differentiate: CT abnormalities are common during viral colds and do not distinguish viral from bacterial sinusitis.
Otitis externa causes canal pain and tragal or pinna tenderness rather than a middle-ear process.
assessment: Ask duration and trajectory, severe fever or facial pain, orbital or neurologic symptoms, hearing or ear discharge and immune status.
Perform otoscopy and nasal or facial assessment rather than diagnosing remotely when findings determine treatment.
workup: Do not routinely image uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis or swab the nasal cavity.
Image sinus disease only when complication or alternate diagnosis is suspected.
management: Provide analgesia, saline and symptom care for viral rhinosinusitis and use antibiotics only when bacterial diagnostic criteria are met.
Use observation or antibiotics for AOM according to age, severity, bilateral disease or otorrhea and reliable follow-up.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical nasal decongestants because of rebound congestion.
Use local antimicrobial recommendations and allergy history when antibiotics are indicated.
redFlags: Severe headache or altered mental status
counselling: Set expectations for viral symptom duration and offer a delayed prescription strategy when appropriate rather than automatic antibiotics.
followUp: Reassess worsening or nonresolving symptoms and hearing or recurrent ear disease when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering sinus CT to decide whether a 4-day cold needs antibiotics.
oneLinePearl: Sinusitis is a time-course diagnosis; AOM is an effusion diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Emergency Medicine Recommendations

title: Red Eye and Vision Loss: Pain Plus Vision Is Urgent
bottomLine: A painless red eye with preserved vision may be conjunctivitis, but eye pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, fixed or irregular pupil, corneal opacity, trauma or sudden vision loss requires urgent ophthalmic evaluation.
recognize: Conjunctivitis usually causes irritation and discharge with relatively preserved visual acuity.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma can cause severe eye or head pain, halos, nausea or vomiting, reduced vision and a poorly reactive pupil.
Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a curtain or field defect and is often painless.
differentiate: Photophobia and deep pain suggest keratitis or uveitis rather than simple conjunctivitis.
Contact-lens wear raises risk of serious microbial keratitis and changes antibiotic and referral urgency.
assessment: Measure visual acuity in each eye, examine pupils, cornea, conjunctiva, extraocular movements and fluorescein when appropriate.
Ask contact lenses, trauma or chemical exposure, headache or nausea, flashes and floaters, and immunosuppression.
workup: Ocular ancillary imaging should be ordered for a clinical indication and does not replace examination, consistent with the Canadian Ophthalmological Society's 2026 Choosing Wisely guidance.
Measure intraocular pressure when acute glaucoma is plausible and safe to do so.
management: Chemical exposure requires immediate copious irrigation before a complete history.
Urgently refer angle-closure glaucoma, keratitis with vision threat, uveitis with severe findings, retinal detachment symptoms, globe injury and sudden unexplained vision loss.
Treat uncomplicated conjunctivitis according to likely viral, bacterial or allergic cause and avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe topical ocular steroids for an undiagnosed red eye because they can worsen infection and other pathology.
Contact-lens-associated infection requires antipseudomonal consideration and lens discontinuation.
counselling: Teach contact-lens hygiene and immediate reassessment for pain or vision change.
followUp: Any red eye that worsens or develops visual symptoms needs reassessment rather than repeated empiric drops.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotic or steroid drops to a painful photophobic red eye without checking visual acuity and cornea.
oneLinePearl: Red eye plus pain or vision change is not routine conjunctivitis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Ophthalmological Society Choosing Wisely Recommendations 2026

title: Male Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms and BPH
bottomLine: Do not assume every older man's urinary symptom is prostate enlargement. Separate storage from voiding symptoms, assess retention, infection, neurologic disease, medications and cancer red flags, then treat based on bother, prostate size or progression risk and patient sexual priorities.
recognize: Voiding symptoms include weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency and straining; storage symptoms include urgency, frequency and nocturia.
Acute urinary retention, recurrent infection, renal dysfunction, bladder stones or gross hematuria are complication patterns needing escalation.
differentiate: Overactive bladder, UTI, diabetes, heart failure or edema, sleep apnea, urethral stricture and neurologic bladder can mimic BPH.
PSA is not a diagnostic test for BPH and should be ordered only after an informed prostate-cancer screening or disease-assessment discussion.
assessment: Assess symptom severity and bother, fluid or caffeine pattern, medications, sexual function, hematuria, infection, neurologic symptoms and prostate-cancer risk.
Perform abdominal or genital and rectal examination when indicated and assess post-void residual when retention is plausible.
workup: Urinalysis is useful to identify hematuria or infection; renal function, PSA, ultrasound or uroflow are selective rather than automatic for every uncomplicated case.
management: Use watchful waiting and lifestyle measures for mild nonbothersome symptoms.

Alpha-blockers improve symptoms quickly but do not shrink the prostate; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are useful for enlarged prostates and reduce progression over time; combination therapy is appropriate in selected higher-risk patients.
Refer or intervene for complications, refractory symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty.
medicationSafety: Alpha-blockers can cause orthostatic hypotension and ejaculatory effects; assess falls risk.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors affect PSA interpretation and can cause sexual adverse effects.
redFlags: Abnormal prostate exam or concerning cancer features
counselling: Ask whether symptom relief, sexual function or avoiding procedures matters most because treatment tradeoffs differ.
followUp: Reassess symptom burden, BP or orthostasis, retention and medication benefit or adverse effects.
examTrap: Ordering a PSA and starting a prostate drug without first determining whether the symptoms are storage, voiding, infectious or neurologic.
oneLinePearl: LUTS is a syndrome; BPH is only one cause.
